2025_112_elementary_writing_materials_ad.paragraph: A Troy School District curriculum recommendation dated May 2025, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Lisa McDonald, presenting the K-5 elementary writing materials review and adoption proposal. Following a review that began in September 2024 and expanded a literacy leadership team to over 100 members in Spring 2025, the district recommends adopting The Writing Units of Study 2024, 2025, which 90% of the team chose as its top choice. The district's last writing adoption was in 2016; resources are to be available on the first day of school for the 2025-26 academic year.
2025_112_elementary_writing_materials_ad.page:
**Document**
Elementary Writing Materials Adoption, May 2025, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Lisa McDonald for the Troy School District.

**Rationale**
Troy regularly reviews curricular materials and has updated its philosophy to look comprehensively at programming — instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data — rather than simply seeking new materials. CORE ELA programs have supported the five pillars of literacy (phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension) but historically offered limited support for writing instruction, so Troy has consistently implemented an additional writing curriculum alongside any reading program. The last writing adoption was in 2016.

**Comprehensive literacy system background**
Sections describe a strong elementary literacy leadership team; a professional learning community using common prep time, peer and vertical observations, district job-embedded lab days, and collaborative walk-throughs; high-quality classroom instruction with new-teacher onboarding in literacy, assessment and MTSS, district PD on handwriting, phonics and upper-grade word work/spelling, and Summer Homegrown Institutes; a system for assessing and monitoring progress (citing Afflerbach, 2007); effective and timely intervention within MTSS; family and community involvement; and access to high-quality preschool.

**Review process**
Fall 2024: a preschool-to-12th-grade literacy leadership meeting; expansion of job-embedded learning around writing instruction to an additional project school; ongoing PD in upper-grades word study/spelling, K-2 handwriting, norming and scoring of writing samples, thin slicing, and writing/phonics assessment; training for literacy specialists and a cohort of teacher consultants and resource room teachers on writing intervention. Spring 2025: the literacy leadership team expanded to over 100 members including representatives from all grade levels in each building, principals, literacy specialists, ELD specialists, special education, media specialists, and Teaching and Learning.

**Research and review tools**
Professional texts studied included "Creating a Classroom Vision for Teaching Writing" by Steve Graham (International Literacy Association), "Why Writing Workshops Work" by Zaner-Bloser, "Writing for Life: The Evidence Base for Powerful Writing Instruction" by Marisa Stukey, PhD and Elyse Eidman-Asdahl, PhD (National Writing Project), and "Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers" from the What Works Clearinghouse (Institute of Education Sciences). Score cards and rubrics consulted were EdReports, the NYU Culturally Responsive Curriculum Score Card, The Reading League, and Knowledge Matters, alongside Michigan Writing and Language Standards. Data reviewed included demographic, process, perception (family and staff survey), and academic data (M-STEP target analysis and student writing samples), referencing "Beyond Testing" by Deborah Meier.

**Programs reviewed and team top-choice results**

| Program | Top choice |
|---|---|
| Writing by Design | 0% |
| Step-Up to Writing | 0% |
| Being a Writer | 4% |
| Benchmark Education Writing Workshop | 6% |
| Writing Units of Study | 90% |

Wit and Wisdom, Heggerty Bridge to Writing (K-3), and i-Ready Ready Writing (2-5) were excluded from review for lack of a cohesive K-5 program or limited rigor in writing instruction.

**Recommendation and early adoption**
The Writing Units of Study 2024, 2025 are recommended. Currently 24 teachers with representation in all 12 buildings and all grade levels are early adopting parts of the updated units, and all K-2 teachers have early adopted at least one updated writing unit. Among the early adoption team, 100% felt the updated Units of Study were helpful to them as teachers and responsive in their instruction, and 100% felt the units had a positive impact on student learning.

**Implementation plan**
All resources will be available for instruction on the first day of school for 2025-26. Training is offered in June and/or August through the Homegrown Institute, with an all-teacher kick-off during back-to-school PD in August 2025, followed by job-embedded professional learning and building-level literacy specialist support. Professional learning will focus on grammar and spelling components in grades 3-5, AI and digital writing in grades 3-5, unpacking new units, embedding phonics assessments and a spelling inventory in the K-5 assessment calendar, thin slicing of writing on-demands with adjusted rubrics, handwriting PD, balancing paper and digital writing, family engagement nights, and continued learning for support staff on writing intervention.
2025_112_elementary_writing_materials_ad.verbose:
Elementary Writing Materials Adoption, dated May 2025 and submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Lisa McDonald, is the Troy School District's recommendation document for a K-5 writing curriculum adoption.

RATIONALE. The district regularly reviews curricular materials and has updated its philosophy since the last curricular adoption, concluding that a comprehensive look at programming — instructional practices, intervention, assessment, and current data — is essential rather than simply seeking new materials. Troy states a commitment to a high-quality writing curriculum aligned with Michigan's writing standards. While CORE ELA programs have supported the five pillars of literacy (phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension), they have historically offered limited support for writing instruction; to address that gap and ensure full rigor with state standards, the district has consistently implemented an additional writing curriculum alongside whatever reading program it has used. The district views writing instruction as equally critical to student success as reading, and is evaluating comprehensive writing programs that function independently of any reading curriculum. The last writing adoption was in 2016.

COMPREHENSIVE LITERACY SYSTEM BACKGROUND. Strong Leadership Team: the elementary literacy leadership team was created with representation of all grade levels, buildings, and departments, and meets regularly to engage in shared learning, review data, reflect on culture, conditions and competencies, and create goals and action plans. Vital Professional Learning Community: changes included utilizing common prep time for teachers, opportunities for teachers to observe grade-level peers, creating vertical observations, providing district job-embedded lab days multiple times a year for each grade level, principal and teaching-and-learning collaborative walk-throughs, administration positioning themselves as co-learners, learning opportunities for diverse learners spanning whole-group, small-group and individual instruction, a focus on active and independent learning, continuous support from literacy specialists at each building, reviewing data and planning for responsive instruction, lab classroom experiences, learning and training at district, county and national levels, and learning partnerships with universities. High Quality Classroom Instruction: support for teacher expertise through professional learning communities and on-site support, high-quality literacy instruction in every classroom, close observation and monitoring of student progress, immediate action and effective intervention when students are not progressing, expanded professional learning, new teacher onboarding in literacy, assessment and MTSS, job-embedded professional learning, district PD around handwriting, phonics, and upper-grade word work/spelling, vertical alignment learning and resource development around writing genres, Summer Homegrown Institutes, and small group intervention training with emphasis on writing support. System for Assessing and Monitoring Programs: the assessment system is rooted in teachers' close observation of students' literacy behaviors with progress monitoring, using both formative and summative assessments, citing Afflerbach, 2007. Effective and Timely Literacy Intervention: early identification and early intervention within the MTSS system, with intervention supplementary to Tier One instruction, short-term, and continuously progress monitored. Family and Community Involvement and Access to High Quality Preschool round out the system, the latter including a streamlined kindergarten transition process, shared learning around early literacy processing with preschool and kindergarten teachers, and instructional coaching.

PROCESS AND SELECTION FOR THE 2024-2025 WRITING CURRICULUM REVIEW. The review began in September 2024 with the Literacy Leadership Team, an interdepartmental, established team with representation from all grade levels and roles. In Fall 2024 the district held a preschool-to-12th-grade literacy leadership meeting to study an overview of the system and future goals, gathered feedback from the K-5 team, expanded job-embedded learning around writing instruction with an additional project school, and continued district professional learning in upper-grades word study/spelling, K-2 handwriting, norming and scoring of writing samples and thin slicing, unpacking writing units and studying student work, and job-embedded learning around writing and phonics assessment and small group instruction. Training also ran for literacy specialists and a cohort of teacher consultants and resource room teachers focused on writing intervention, and all K-5 teachers were updated on the review process. In Spring 2025 the literacy leadership team expanded to over 100 members, made up of representatives from all grade levels in each building, principals, literacy specialists, ELD specialists, special education, media specialists, and Teaching and Learning. Meeting outcomes were reflecting on the current state in writing, reviewing student writing samples from the current year and progressions over time K-5, and shared learning around best practice.

RESEARCH BASE AND REVIEW TOOLS. Texts and sources studied included "Creating a Classroom Vision for Teaching Writing" by Steve Graham, a professor/researcher of 30-plus years published by the International Literacy Association; "Why Writing Workshops Work" by Zaner-Bloser, with underpinnings from researchers over the last 30 years; "Writing for Life: The Evidence Base for Powerful Writing Instruction" by Marisa Stukey, PhD and Elyse Eidman-Asdahl, PhD of the National Writing Project, described as the nation's largest network of teacher-leaders working for almost 50 years; and "Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers," a What Works Clearinghouse practice guide from the Institute of Education Sciences, the statistics, research, and evaluation arm of the U.S. Department of Education, offering four recommendations for improving elementary students' writing. The team created its own rubric around its values in writing instruction matched to the Troy vision and district pillars, and reviewed additional curriculum score cards and rubrics: EdReports, an independent nonprofit reviewing K-12 instructional materials for alignment to standards and usability; the NYU Culturally Responsive Curriculum Score Card, developed by the Education Justice Research and Organizing Collaborative at NYU's Metro Center; The Reading League tool for alignment with the science of reading; and Knowledge Matters for knowledge-building instruction. Michigan Writing and Language Standards were used to match alignment. Data studied included demographic data (current numbers of students served K-5), process data (leadership team and early adopter feedback), perception data (family and staff survey), and academic data (M-STEP target analysis and student writing samples), with a note referencing "Beyond Testing" by Deborah Meier and its seven alternative forms of assessment.

PROGRAMS EXCLUDED AND REVIEWED. Excluded from review for lack of a cohesive K-5 program or limited rigor in writing instruction were Wit and Wisdom, Heggerty Bridge to Writing (K-3), and i-Ready Ready Writing (2-5). Programs reviewed and scored, with the share of the team choosing each as top choice: Writing by Design, 0% — criticized for lacking instructional support, being heavy with worksheets and graphic organizers, focusing primarily on 6 traits, not being robust enough to meet state standards, lacking volume of writing, poor and outdated mentor texts, weak assessments, and lack of professional development. Step-Up to Writing, 0% — a writing process approach with multiple genres not taught until upper grades, students learning within workbooks, students told what to write, weak assessments, no use of mentor texts, and professional development limited to online videos. Being a Writer, 4% — multiple genres taught though lacking literary essay, diverse mentor texts, some grammar and spelling, but workbook-based, lacking teacher resources and differentiation support, with professional learning mostly webinars or study guides. Benchmark Education Writing Workshop, 6% — a workshop model with less time for actual student writing, multiple genres, a grammar component, mentor texts lacking diversity, slower pacing, student workbooks, limited assessment, and no job-embedded professional learning. Writing Units of Study, 90% — a K-5 cohesive curriculum meeting Michigan State Standards, covering narrative, opinion/argumentative, informational, and literary essay genres, with teacher implementation supports, parent communication resources, digital features, an assessment system, access and support for all learners, high-leverage small groups and conferences, built-in professional development, culturally relevant and engaging materials, more support for phonics, spelling, grammar and writing conventions, volume in writing, explicit instruction, responsive teaching and in-the-moment feedback, diverse mentor texts, writing trajectories, writing for real audiences, and leveraging AI as a tool.

FINDINGS FROM THE LEADERSHIP TEAM, K-5 STAFF AND FAMILIES. What is going well and valued: the workshop model providing explicit and responsive teaching; student voice, identity, critical thinking, choice, volume, and variety of genres; alignment to Michigan writing standards; student outcomes in organization, elaboration, and supporting evidence; and real-world connections. Areas for improvement considered during review: grammar, spelling, handwriting, learning for families about the writing process and progression, and deep learning opportunities for special education and support staff. Families were engaged through a feedback survey, information at building PTO meetings, and a family Writing Review Information Night.

MATERIALS RECOMMENDATION. The Writing Units of Study 2024, 2025 are recommended to move forward, with publisher quotes included at the end of the document. Currently 24 teachers with representation in all 12 buildings and all grade levels are early adopting parts of the updated writing Units of Study, and all K-2 teachers have early adopted at least one updated writing unit. Early adoption team feedback reports that 100% of the teachers felt the updated Units of Study were helpful to them as teachers and responsive in their instruction, and 100% felt the updated units had a positive impact on their students' learning. Teacher testimonials praise the grammar lessons, simplified and explicit mini lessons, short and manageable spelling and grammar lessons, spelling charts, digital access and E-books, shorter and more student-friendly writing checklists, more engaging mentor texts, the literary essay unit, the color layout of the books, the purposeful integration of grammar and phonics, and the "Supporting All Writers" small group book.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN. All resources will be available for instruction on the first day of school for the 2025-26 academic year. Teachers may receive training on the updated changes in June and/or August through the Homegrown Institute, and all teachers will participate in a kick-off during back-to-school PD in August 2025 focused on the writing curriculum. Teachers will participate in job-embedded professional learning with literacy specialist support at each building. Professional learning will focus on newer grammar and spelling components in grades 3-5, AI and digital writing in grades 3-5, unpacking new units to grade levels, embedding phonics assessments and spelling inventory in the K-5 assessment calendar, continued thin slicing of writing on-demands with adjusted writing rubrics, ongoing review of PD around handwriting, balance of writing on paper and digital writing, more family engagement nights, and continuous learning for support staff around writing intervention.

2025_113_aarc_feedback.paragraph: A Troy School District presentation on Attendance Area Review Community Feedback, prepared for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop, reporting results of five community listening sessions and two surveys and laying out projected middle school enrollments under each boundary scenario. The adult survey drew 1,777 responses, of which 70.1% favored some version of Option C, and the student survey drew 1,229 responses. Under existing boundaries the four middle schools held 2,940 pupils in December 2024, projected to fall to 2,526 pupils by 2027.
2025_113_aarc_feedback.page:
**Document**
Attendance Area Review Community Feedback, Troy School District, presented for the May 6, 2025 Board of Education workshop (PDF version).

**Phases**
Phase 1 Discovery — committee formed; research, analysis and planning; potential recommendations developed. Phase 2 Recommendation (January) — committee provides the Board with options; Board determines whether to proceed. Phase 3 Feedback (March-April) — four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, plus a community survey. Phase 4 Determination (May) — TSD provides the Board a summary of feedback and the Board determines any future changes.

**AARC goals**
Goal 1: right-size middle schools, equal student ratios. Goal 2: resolve double splits. Goal 3: no impact on high schools.

**Community meetings**
Five community meetings were held, one at each middle school with two at Larson due to spring break. Feedback themes: preferred time to split students (ES to MS or MS to HS), moving high school boundaries, reducing middle school splits another way, managing Somerset Apartments other than having them attend six schools, how long legacy status would be provided and whether elementary students would be included, considering other options, mental health and social/emotional impact of an MS-to-HS split under Option C, and offering open enrollment for Larson, Smith and others.

**Feedback form (5 community meetings)**
31 responses; 74% of respondents from Troy Union. Open-ended tallies: TU to Larson 6; TU to Troy High 3; TU to Smith 3; consider other options 8; mental health impacts from splits 5; move HS boundaries 3; remove all splits 3; no MS to HS splits 5.

**Adult survey — 1,777 responses**
90.7% were a parent/guardian of a current student. Highest respondent student attendance: Troy High 328, Larson 327, Athens 297, Boulan Park 266, Hamilton 240; live in Somerset Apartments 53. 60.8% were familiar with the AARC process, most having read about it on the website and/or weekly newsletter. 70.1% favored some version of Option C, with Option C at 31.8%; 76.1% did not have an opinion or did not want the Board to consider any other option. Additional unlabeled percentage callouts: 73% and 52.3% important; 80.7% and 76% important; 81.3% and 76.5% important; ES to MS 72.7% and Yes & No Preference 51.5%; increase SOC 53% and allow open enrollment 63.2%.

**Student survey — 1,229 responses**

**Presentation**
Secondary Math Updates, Troy School District, May 6, 2025.

**Vision for mathematics**
All students are doers of mathematics; the program's purpose is to cultivate students' positive mathematical identities so that all students develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics. Sourced to NCTM (2020), Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics.

**Professional learning**
The 2024 Math Summer Institute; back-to-school professional learning days; onsite learning with Illustrative Math and NWEA; monthly job-embedded professional learning with Honors Algebra 1; full days of learning during October, January, and March district professional learning; Math Specialists attending the IM coaching institute; and a full-time Math Specialist in each building to unpack units, co-plan, co-teach, coach teachers, and do intervention with struggling students.

**Support for families**
Every IM unit includes Family Support Materials describing the big ideas in plain language, with an overview of the mathematics, what to expect as learning deepens, and conversation-prompting questions. Every IM lesson includes a lesson summary in student-friendly language, useful for absences and for families. A Family Math Night was held for families with students in Math 7.

**Honors Algebra 1 enrollment**

| Course | 2021-2022 | 2022-2023 | 2023-2024 | 2024-2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 7 | 2% | 1% | 1% | 8% |
| Honors Algebra 1, Grade 8 | 36% | 37% | 35% | 50% |

**NWEA MAP Growth**
MAP Growth is a computer-adaptive assessment used in K-12 schools by over 16 million students, nationally normed and standards aligned; MAP stands for Measures of Academic Progress. In 2024/25 all students in grades 6-8 and students enrolled in Algebra 1 took MAP Growth in the Fall and Spring, with Math 7 students also testing in Winter to provide an additional data point when choosing Math 8 or Honors Algebra 1. In 2025/26 all students in grades 6-8 and students in all levels of Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 will test in Fall, Winter, and Spring. MAP Growth provides RIT (Rasch Unit) scores indicating instructional level, growth over time, projected growth against national norms, and disaggregated data. Next steps: use as a screener for intervention and extension, establish cohort data for grade-level growth, compare Fall to Spring, use district data with teachers in late summer, hold a Summer 2025 Data Retreat with administrators, and continue professional learning in 2025-26.

**Student perception data (1,932 respondents)**
Celebrations: 93% said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% agreed with "I know I can be good at math"; 79% feel prepared for the next level of math; 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges: 34% would like more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% do not enjoy learning math; 24% said the lessons are too easy; 17% said the lessons are too hard.

**Teacher perception data (19 respondents)**
Celebrations: 95% say they are comfortable navigating the resource; 79% say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Challenges: 37% need more resources for families; 42% are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Written comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading/comprehension skills, more supplemental practice, closer alignment between assessments and learning activities, guidance on what can be combined or eliminated, and more at-home written examples.

**Distinguished math students**
In the 2025-26 school year a committee including a variety of stakeholders will be formed to investigate how to recognize distinguished middle school math students, considering extensions in and outside the classroom; information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.

MAP Growth is established as a screener to identify students who may need intervention and students who may need extension; the district will establish cohort data to identify grade-level growth; comparisons from Fall to Spring will be made, with spring testing happening at the time of the presentation; the aim is maintaining high levels of performance and growing student performance; district data will be used late summer with teachers; a Data Retreat with administrators is planned for Summer 2025; and continued professional learning with teachers is planned for the 2025-26 school year.

STUDENT PERCEPTION DATA (1,932). Celebrations reported: 93% of students said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone; 87% of students said they had lots of opportunities to interact with each other; 88% agreed that in their math class it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time; 90% of students agreed with the statement "I know I can be good at math"; 79% of students feel prepared for the next level of math; and 59% said the lessons are "just right for them." Challenges reported: 34% of students would like to receive more specific feedback on how to improve their work; 45% of students do not enjoy learning math; 24% of students said the lessons are too easy; and 17% of students said the lessons are too hard.

STUDENT VOICE. Quoted student comments include enjoying interactions with peers and being at a level where "the math isn't too easy or too hard"; a teacher explaining math equations with real-life examples; appreciation that there are different ways to learn math; and feeling confident enough to raise a hand without being judged and working with friends. Suggestions from students include adding a difficulty level to assignments to show improvement, more interactive projects or activities so class does not get boring, a pre-test so the teacher understands what students know, more repetitive practice per activity to aid retention before tests, and learning more things that will be used in real life.

TEACHER PERCEPTION DATA (19). Celebrations: 95% of teachers say they are comfortable navigating the resource, and 79% of teachers say they have the tools they need to accurately measure student progress. Quoted teacher comments praise that there is not just one way to learn most content, that the curriculum figures out the "why," the conceptual content, the "are you ready for more" tasks, the collaborative tasks, the emphasis on getting students to talk and write math, the connection of math to real-life situations, and the low-floor approach that is inviting for struggling students. Challenges: 37% of teachers need more resources for families, and 42% of teachers are using the IM Instructional Routines that support student access. Teacher comments request more support for ELD students and students with low reading and comprehension skills, noting that reading a problem three times is not always doable or helpful; more supplemental practice to solidify concepts; assessments that match more of what the learning activities look like throughout lessons; more guidance on what can be combined or eliminated from lessons or units; and more at-home resources with written-out examples beyond the online workbook and videos.

RECOGNIZING DISTINGUISHED MATH STUDENTS. In the 2025-26 school year the district will form a committee that includes a variety of stakeholders to investigate how it might recognize distinguished middle school math students. As extensions are considered, the district will look to include opportunities in and outside of the classroom. Information will be posted on the district website and communicated through the Troy Newsletter.
